verses.verse:
गोला कारे तु वादी स्यात् संवादी त्वर्ध गोलके।
अर्धद्वये विवादीस्या न्निश्चिन्हास्त्वनुवादिनः।१२३।
verses.text: A note in a circle is the vādī (principal note); one in a half circle is the saṃvādī (consonant second note); one within two halves is the vivādī (dissonant note); and the unmarked notes are the anuvādī (assonant notes).

verses.verse:
दण्डा कारेण संबद्धौ स्वरौ संगतये मतौ।
सर्प चिन्हाः स्वराः ह्यत्र भवेयुः कम्पिताः सदा।१२४।
verses.text: Two notes joined by a staff-shaped sign (daṇḍākāra) are meant to go together (saṅgati, companionship of notes). Notes here with the snake sign (sarpa cihna) are always to be oscillated (kampita).

verses.verse:
तीव्रादीनां तु संकेतः कृतो नारायणैः पुरा।
दृष्ट्वारोहेऽवरोहे च ज्ञातव्यास्ते मनीषिभि।१२५।
verses.text: The signs for tīvra and the other [altered] notes were made long ago by Nārāyaṇa [Bhātkhaṇḍe ji]. The wise should learn them by seeing them in the ascent and the descent.

commentary.text: In the ślokas above, some symbolic signs for the notes have been given. On the basis of these signs we shall get a general introduction to rāgas through their āroha avaroha (ascent and descent) alone. For a detailed introduction, other śāstras (treatises) of music may be consulted.
(1) Take the note written inside a circle as the vādī (principal note), e.g. - [Ga]
(2) Notes written in a half circle are to be regarded as saṃvādī (consonant second note), e.g. - °Ni
(3) Take notes placed within two half circles as vivādī (dissonant note), e.g. - °Ma°
(4) Where in the ascent we mark Ga Ma Pa Dha in this form, the companionship (saṅgati) of those two notes will be rāga-identifying.
(5) Take the notes that have a snake-like sign beneath them as oscillated (āndolita) in that rāga, e.g. Ga
Apart from these, the signs for tīvra and other notes will be taken from the works of the late Śrī Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇ Bhātkhaṇḍe ji, which were settled long ago.

So if, in the following rāgas, we elaborate the notes keeping in mind the signs marked in the ārohāvaroha (ascent and descent), we shall have greater success in the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of the rāga. First of all let us look at Rāga Bhūpālī, which is both sweet and easy on the bansī (bamboo bānsurī).

Here the book has not been lengthened by giving the svara vistāra (elaboration of notes) of more rāgas, but the scientific basis of the method of ālāpa (svara vistāra) has been made clear. From the elaborations above it has become clear to us that the sign of nyāsa (resting note) and vinyāsa (phrase-ending note) can be used in the nyāsa, and the sign (mark) of vinyāsa in the vinyāsa. In other books nyāsa and vinyāsa have one and the same sign, e.g. - ṆiReGa, Ni Ma′ Re Ga, Re Ga Re Ma′ Ga and so on. But for apanyāsa (intermediate resting note) a sign of broken shape (khaṇḍākāra) has been given, e.g. - Ni Re Ga Ma′ Pa – Pa Ma′ Ga, Ga Ma′ Dha Pa – Re Ga and so on. For sanyāsa (ending note of the first phrase) all treatises give the sign of the full stop. So if, by the method described earlier, we understand the separate importance of the notes of rāgas and do the svara vistāra ourselves, and keep testing whether it is right or wrong by looking at the svara vistāras given in other books, it is possible that our sādhanā (practice) will succeed.
